nodes.question: How are the law enforcement penalties viewed in relation to their effectiveness against illegal hunting?
nodes.answer: The law enforcement penalties were considered less deterrent, leading most hunters to intend to continue with illegal hunting.
nodes.paragraph: The common hunting methods reported were hunting with dogs (87%), and snaring (65%). Targeted animal species included impala (96%), wildebeest (53%), eland (53%), African buffalo (51%) among other 12 animal species. Illegal bushmeat hunting was generally conducted all year round. The law enforcement penalties were considered less deterrent, and most of the hunters intended to continue with illegal hunting. Measures suggested to minimize illegal bushmeat hunting in the SVC included investing and strengthening wildlife lawenforcement, provision of community conservation-based incentives and enhancing environmental education and awareness. nodes.question: What are the consequences faced by illegal hunters upon arrest?
nodes.answer: Illegal hunters may be subjected to fines and other forms of punishments.
nodes.paragraph: Upon arrest the illegal hunters may be subjected to nes and other forms of punishments (Duffy et al. 2019 ). Regardless of having these numerous risks, illegal bushmeat hunting is prevalent in many protected areas because the potential bene its accrued by illegal hunters outweigh the costs (Knapp 2012 ). To date, various bottom-up and top-down strategies have been implemented to reduce the rate and intensity of illegalhunting. While top-down measures like law enforcement are critical in reducing illegal activities and protecting wildlife resources, their effectiveness is highly debated(Duffy et al. 2019 ; Witter 2021 ). Nevertheless, it S worth noting that, bushmeat poaching is particularly prevalent inregions characterized by inadequate law enforcement (der Westhuizen and Vliet 2012 ). Generally, wildlife crimes in several countries are con- sidered as of low priority (Lindsey et al. 2012 ). The gazetted penalties like warning, community service and low value nes do not re ect the value of wildlife resources being lost (Lindsey, et al. 2011b ).
